text: André Lallemand (French pronunciation: [ɑ̃dʁe lalmɑ̃]; September 29, 1904 – March 24, 1978)[1] was a French astronomer and director of the Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris. He made significant contributions to the development of photomultipliers for astronomical applications and invented the "electronic telescope" (or Lallemand camera). He received the Lalande Prize from the French Academy of Sciences in 1938[2] and the Eddington Medal from the Royal Astronomical Society in 1962 for his scientific achievements. Lallemand served as President of the Société astronomique de France (SAF), the French astronomical society, from 1960 to 1962.[3] The crater Lallemand on the Moon is named in his honor, and the French Academy of Sciences bestows a biennial award in astronomy known as the "Prix Lallemand".
